disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, leading to significant distress or impairment. Individuals typically engage in repetitive behaviors or mental acts (such as mirror checking, camouflaging, comparing, or seeking reassurance) in response to these concerns. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood and the course is usually chronic, waxing and waning with stress and life transitions. BDD is distinct from normal appearance dissatisfaction and from eating disorders by the intensity of the preoccupation, the presence of time‑consuming repetitive behaviors, and the focus on specific perceived defects rather than primarily on weight or shape.

narrative.personality: He is a methodical yet restless full‑stack developer whose chronic anxiety fuels meticulous planning, intense focus on details, and a tendency to over‑prepare for situations.
narrative.stressor: His concerns about his appearance intensified after his company shifted to a more public‑facing culture, where developers were increasingly expected to appear on client video calls, record demo videos, and maintain active professional social media profiles. A few offhand comments from coworkers about looking tired on camera and a joking remark about his "developer look" during a team photo made him acutely self‑conscious, especially given his long‑standing anxious, detail‑oriented temperament. Over time, prepping for any situation that involved being seen—team photos, remote meetings, even casual outings with his board‑game group—began to consume more of his evenings and encroach on his hobby projects and volunteering, causing him to miss deadlines and avoid opportunities for visibility at work. He finally sought psychiatric help when he realized that his preoccupation with how he looked on camera and in public was undermining his performance reviews, disrupting his sleep, and making him cancel hikes and social plans at the last minute.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m spending way too much time getting ready and checking how I look before any video call or social thing, and it’s starting to mess with my work and my life.”

narrative.personality: He is a disciplined, detail‑oriented medical records specialist with a quiet competitive streak who values order, health, and modest comforts like fine coffee and nature walks.
narrative.stressor: In his late fifties, he underwent minor dermatologic procedures for sun‑damaged skin on his face and scalp, which coincided with his increasing focus on aging and health as he approached retirement. Although his physicians reassured him that the procedures were successful and left only minimal changes, he became convinced that the treated areas looked disfiguring and that others at work and on the hiking trails were noticing and judging him. His naturally meticulous and perfectionistic style, honed through decades of scrutinizing medical records, shifted toward an ever‑narrowing focus on perceived imperfections in his face and scalp, gradually crowding out his enjoyment of bird‑watching groups, woodworking meetups, and even routine errands. He eventually agreed to seek psychiatric evaluation after his supervisor and a close hiking companion both expressed concern that he was turning down consulting opportunities, avoiding in‑person meetings, and spending so much time fixated on his appearance that it was interfering with his work transition plans and daily functioning.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve gotten obsessed with checking the spots on my face and head after some skin treatments, and it’s taking over my days.”

narrative.personality: He is a contemplative, intellectually inclined clergy member who is creative and warm but chronically worried and prone to over‑committing to community projects.
narrative.stressor: His appearance concerns crystallized after a series of livestreamed services and recorded sermons during a period when his congregation shifted heavily to online worship, making him repeatedly view himself on camera and in promotional materials. Parishioners’ well‑intentioned comments about how he “looked tired” or how the camera “adds 10 pounds,” combined with his own longstanding self‑consciousness and reflective temperament, led him to scrutinize his image obsessively when editing videos or reviewing photos for church newsletters. Over the next few years, what began as a desire to be a presentable spiritual leader gradually morphed into a consuming preoccupation that made sermon preparation and pastoral visits increasingly stressful, as he devoted more time and mental energy to worrying about how he appeared than to the content of his ministry. He finally sought psychiatric help when he noticed he was rearranging his schedule around avoiding being photographed or filmed, delaying community events, and feeling that his ability to lead authentically was being compromised by constant worries about his physical appearance.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Preparing for any service or event that might be recorded or photographed has turned into this endless routine of checking how I look, and it’s getting in the way of my ministry.”
